claims.text: Chemical disorder in refractory high-entropy alloys creates local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions produce a heterogeneous distribution of elastic moduli.
The disorder-induced local elastic heterogeneity strengthens the alloy mechanically.
The disorder-induced local elastic heterogeneity reduces thermoelastic softening.
Enhancing short-range chemical order narrows the distribution of local elastic constants.
Enhancing short-range chemical order increases macroscopic stiffness relative to a fully random alloy of the same composition.
Enhancing short-range chemical order reduces the coefficient of thermal expansion relative to a fully random alloy of the same composition.
Chemically induced lattice distortions create local variations in bond stiffness.
In the fully random state, local bond-stiffness variations lower the average elastic response.
In the fully random state, local bond-stiffness variations produce more pronounced thermoelastic softening.
Reducing the heterogeneity of local elastic constants enhances overall stiffness at high temperature.
Reducing the heterogeneity of local elastic constants reduces thermal expansion at high temperature.
An SRO-enhanced alloy will have lower simulated dislocation mobility than the fully disordered baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies when the alloy remains single phase at service temperature and phase transformations and grain-boundary effects do not dominate its response.
The magnitude of the predicted effects depends on short-range-order level, alloy composition, and simulation parameters.
